newsitem.title: USA: US fund manager seeks expertise from trading pits.
newsitem.headline: US fund manager seeks expertise from trading pits.

text.p: A minute can be an eternity in the world of futures trading. It can mean the difference between a fortune and bankruptcy. Someone who survives 20 years in the ephemeral trading pits is therefore a sought-after commodity.
Futures fund manager Jim Moore for the past eight years has eschewed the traditional office-bound trading adviser to manage his portfolios in favor of veterans of the rough-and-tumble pits.

In an industry where traders in exchange pits are predominantly young and brash, Moore seeks out those with at least 10 and preferably 20 years of trading floor experience. Those traders then use their own trading methods to manage segments of Moore's funds.
Moore heads DGM Investments Inc of Greenwood Lake, New York, managing private investment pools and joint ventures that rank among the better-performing domestic and offshore funds.

Managed Account Reports, which publishes returns of managed futures funds, ranked Moore's flagship CTP (Cotton Trading Partners) Fund third of 410 futures funds and pools for its performance for the three years ended August 31.
The cornerstone of Moore's philosophy is found in the trading pits. He builds each segment of DGM's funds around a particular pit trader's strategy and expertise.
"It was clear to me where the best traders were, and the best traders were on the floors of the exchanges," Moore said in a recent interview.
Avoiding flash-in-the-pan types, he seeks traders with longevity, the veterans who control the risks they take.

"Floor trading is a young man's game," Moore explained. "Once they are 42 or 44 or 46 they have built into them probably the best risk-control structure of anyone around," Moore said. "If you can maintain life on the floor for 20 years you really know how to manage your risk."
With 31 veteran traders, Moore oversees $112 million in five offshore funds and three domestic funds. DGM traders must put money of their own in the pool they trade and cannot trade other accounts.

Moore's career has taken him from Shearson's futures asset management division, to consultant to the chairman of Merrill Lynch's futures department, managing director of Thomson McKinnon's Futures Management department and ultimately, chief of DGM Investments funds.
In his 29 years in the business, Moore said he has learned the value of position traders whose skills were honed on the floor.
"Consistency matters and risk control matters much more than people realize," he said. "There's always another good trade coming, but there's not always another good trade manager."
Among his funds, Moore said his Standard and Poor's 500 options fund was up 38 percent this year through July, while his Treasury bond futures fund was up 36 percent.

Moore said the CTP fund was up about eight percent through July after posting a year-to-date return of 31 percent by the end of March. September so far has shaped up well for the fund and he expects CTP to regain the pace of earlier this year, he said.
